claim: CyaA is a key virulence factor of the whooping cough agent Bordetella pertussis.
source: Here we found that the adenylate cyclase toxin (CyaA), a key virulence factor of the whooping cough agent Bordetella pertussis, preferentially binds an inactive form of the integrin complement receptor 3 (CR3), using a site outside of its I-domain.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about CyaA.

claim: CyaA preferentially binds an inactive form of CR3.
source: Here we found that the adenylate cyclase toxin (CyaA), a key virulence factor of the whooping cough agent Bordetella pertussis, preferentially binds an inactive form of the integrin complement receptor 3 (CR3), using a site outside of its I-domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: CyaA binds CR3 using a site outside of its I-domain.
source: Here we found that the adenylate cyclase toxin (CyaA), a key virulence factor of the whooping cough agent Bordetella pertussis, preferentially binds an inactive form of the integrin complement receptor 3 (CR3), using a site outside of its I-domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by domain swapping experiments in Figure 1.

claim: CyaA binding did not trigger downstream signaling of CR3 in human monocytes.
source: CyaA binding did not trigger downstream signaling of CR3 in human monocytes and CyaA-catalyzed elevation of cAMP effectively blocked CR3 signaling initiated by a natural ligand.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by Syk phosphorylation experiments in Figure 6.

claim: CyaA-catalyzed elevation of cAMP effectively blocked CR3 signaling initiated by a natural ligand.
source: CyaA binding did not trigger downstream signaling of CR3 in human monocytes and CyaA-catalyzed elevation of cAMP effectively blocked CR3 signaling initiated by a natural ligand.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experiments in Figure 7.

claim: There are 18 different alpha subunits and 8 beta subunits of integrins that combine in 24 known combinations in mammals.
source: There are 18 different alpha subunits and 8 beta subunits that combine in a limited number of combinations of which 24 are currently known in mammals (Tan, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tan, 2012.

claim: Nine of the eighteen integrin alpha subunits harbor a conserved I-domain that is crucial for binding of endogenous ligands.
source: Nine of the eighteen integrin alpha subunits harbor a conserved I (inserted)-domain that is crucial for binding of endogenous ligands (Johnson and Chouhan, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Johnson and Chouhan, 2014.

claim: Four integrin alpha subunits (αD, αL, αM and αX) form heterodimers exclusively with the β2 subunit.
source: Four of these integrin alpha subunits (αD, αL, αM and αX) form heterodimers exclusively with the β2 subunit, thus forming the αDβ2 (CD11d/CD18), αLβ2 (CD11a/CD18, LFA-1), αMβ2 (CD11b/CD18, complement receptor 3 (CR3), Mac1) and αXβ2 (CD11c/CD18, CR4, p150/195) integrins, respectively (Arnaout, 1990; Mazzone and Ricevuti, 1995; Sanchez-Madrid, 1983; Tan, 2012; Van der Vieren et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: β2 integrins have specialized roles in immune and inflammatory responses.
source: The β2 integrins have specialized roles in immune and inflammatory responses and, like other integrins, employ a two-step mechanism of bi-directional signal transmission between the interior of cells and the extracellular milieu (Anthis and Campbell, 2011; Tan, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anthis and Campbell, 2011 and Tan, 2012.

claim: Integrins employ a two-step mechanism of bi-directional signal transmission between the interior of cells and the extracellular milieu.
source: The β2 integrins have specialized roles in immune and inflammatory responses and, like other integrins, employ a two-step mechanism of bi-directional signal transmission between the interior of cells and the extracellular milieu (Anthis and Campbell, 2011; Tan, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anthis and Campbell, 2011 and Tan, 2012.

claim: Inside-out signaling is initiated through rearrangement of the integrin molecule from an inactive (bent, closed, resting, low-affinity) conformation to an active (extended, open, high-affinity) conformation.
source: Upon activation by various intracellular signals, the inside-out signaling is initiated through rearrangement of the integrin molecule from an inactive (bent, closed, resting, low-affinity) conformation to an active (extended, open, high-affinity) conformation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about integrin signaling.

claim: Ligand binding triggers outside-in signaling of the extended integrins through activation of Src family tyrosine kinases.
source: Subsequent ligand binding triggers outside-in signaling of the extended integrins through activation of Src family tyrosine kinases (Jakus et al., 2007; Mócsai et al., 2002; 2010; Schymeinsky et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Src kinases phosphorylate tyrosine residues within the immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM) on ITAM-containing transmembrane adaptor proteins.
source: Src kinases phosphorylate tyrosine residues within the so-called immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM), on the cytoplasmic face of ITAM-containing transmembrane adaptor proteins, such as DAP12 or the FcR γ-chain (FcRγ) (Jakus et al., 2007; Mócsai et al., 2006; 2010; Schymeinsky et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Phosphorylated ITAM motifs serve as docking sites for the tandem phosphotyrosine-binding Src homology 2 (SH2) domains of Syk.
source: These serve as docking sites for the tandem phosphotyrosine-binding Src homology 2 (SH2) domains of the non-receptor spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) (Jakus et al., 2007; Mócsai et al., 2006; 2010; Schymeinsky et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Recruitment and activation of Syk leads to assembly of a multi-protein signaling complex that initiates downstream signaling.
source: Recruitment and activation of Syk then leads to assembly of a multi-protein signaling complex that contains cytosolic Syk-binding molecules and initiates further downstream signaling, ultimately triggering various cellular responses that play a central role in the innate immune defense to infection (Mócsai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mócsai et al., 2010.

claim: CR3 is used as receptor by the adenylate cyclase toxin-hemolysin (CyaA) of Bordetella pertussis.
source: The β2 integrin complement receptor 3 (CR3) is used as receptor by the 1706 residue-long RTX (Repeats in ToXin) adenylate cyclase toxin-hemolysin (CyaA, ACT, or AC-Hly) of Bordetella pertussis, which plays a crucial role in virulence and immune evasion of the whooping cough agent (Goodwin and Weiss, 1990; Guermonprez et al., 2001; Khelef et al., 1992; Vojtova et al., 2006; Weiss et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CyaA plays a crucial role in virulence and immune evasion of the whooping cough agent.
source: The β2 integrin complement receptor 3 (CR3) is used as receptor by the 1706 residue-long RTX (Repeats in ToXin) adenylate cyclase toxin-hemolysin (CyaA, ACT, or AC-Hly) of Bordetella pertussis, which plays a crucial role in virulence and immune evasion of the whooping cough agent (Goodwin and Weiss, 1990; Guermonprez et al., 2001; Khelef et al., 1992; Vojtova et al., 2006; Weiss et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Upon binding to CR3, CyaA penetrates myeloid phagocytes and paralyzes their bactericidal functions by catalyzing uncontrolled conversion of cytosolic ATP to cAMP.
source: Upon binding to CR3, CyaA penetrates myeloid phagocytes and paralyzes their bactericidal functions by catalyzing uncontrolled conversion of cytosolic ATP to the key signaling molecule cAMP (Confer and Eaton, 1982; Guermonprez et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Confer and Eaton, 1982 and Guermonprez et al., 2001.

claim: CyaA hijacks maturation and proinflammatory signaling of CR3-expressing dendritic cells.
source: The toxin also hijacks maturation and proinflammatory signaling of CR3-expressing dendritic cells and it likely subverts antigen presentation and induction of adaptive T cell immune responses to bacterial infection by intraepithelial dendritic cells of host respiratory mucosa (Bagley et al., 2002; Boschwitz et al., 1997; Boyd et al., 2005; Fedele et al., 2010; Hickey et al., 2008; Njamkepo et al., 2000; Ross et al., 2004; Spensieri et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CyaA likely subverts antigen presentation and induction of adaptive T cell immune responses to bacterial infection by intraepithelial dendritic cells of host respiratory mucosa.
source: The toxin also hijacks maturation and proinflammatory signaling of CR3-expressing dendritic cells and it likely subverts antigen presentation and induction of adaptive T cell immune responses to bacterial infection by intraepithelial dendritic cells of host respiratory mucosa (Bagley et al., 2002; Boschwitz et al., 1997; Boyd et al., 2005; Fedele et al., 2010; Hickey et al., 2008; Njamkepo et al., 2000; Ross et al., 2004; Spensieri et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and is stated as a likely mechanism.

claim: CHO cells expressing human CR3 can be used as a suitable model for studying the interaction of CyaA with CR3.
source: It was previously shown that Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells expressing human CR3 can be used as a suitable model for studying the interaction of CyaA with CR3 (Guermonprez et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guermonprez et al., 2001.

claim: CR3 (CD11b/CD18) expressed by CHO cells allowed the binding and cAMP-elevating (cytotoxic) activities of CyaA.
source: Indeed, CR3 (CD11b/CD18) expressed by CHO cells allowed the binding and cAMP-elevating (cytotoxic) activities of CyaA, while the highly homologous CR4 (CD11c/CD18) was unable to bind CyaA despite sharing the same β2 (CD18) subunit with CR3 (Guermonprez et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guermonprez et al., 2001.

claim: CR4 (CD11c/CD18) was unable to bind CyaA despite sharing the same β2 (CD18) subunit with CR3.
source: Indeed, CR3 (CD11b/CD18) expressed by CHO cells allowed the binding and cAMP-elevating (cytotoxic) activities of CyaA, while the highly homologous CR4 (CD11c/CD18) was unable to bind CyaA despite sharing the same β2 (CD18) subunit with CR3 (Guermonprez et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guermonprez et al., 2001.

claim: Replacement of the segment containing residues 614 to 682 of CD11b by the corresponding portion of CD11c caused a sharp, about ten-fold decrease of CyaA binding to CHO cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, replacement of the segment containing residues 614 to 682 (segment 614-682) of CD11b by the corresponding portion of CD11c caused a sharp, about ten-fold decrease of CyaA binding to the CHO-CD11b614-682c/CD18 transfectants, as compared to cells expressing intact CR3 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CyaA binding was partially reduced on cells expressing CR3 chimeras having the residues 33 to 115, 342 to 424, or 686 to 1152 of CD11b replaced by the corresponding segments of CD11c.
source: CyaA binding was also partially reduced on cells expressing CR3 chimeras having the residues 33 to 115 (72 ± 6%), 342 to 424 (61 ± 10%), or 686 to 1152 (89 ± 11%) of CD11b replaced by the corresponding segments of CD11c, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CyaA binding and subsequent intoxication of cells by cAMP were neither reduced by swapping of the homologous I-domain regions between CD11b and CD11c nor upon removal of the entire I-domain of CD11b.
source: Surprisingly, CyaA binding and subsequent intoxication of cells by cAMP were neither reduced by swapping of the homologous I-domain regions between CD11b and CD11c (CD11b120-272c and CD11b275-339c), nor upon removal of the entire I-domain of CD11b (CD11bΔ164-339) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: CyaA does not bind CR3 through the I-domain.
source: This demonstrates that CyaA does not bind CR3 through the I-domain and rather recognizes the segment containing residues 614 to 682 that encompasses the C-terminal end of the last repeat of the β-propeller domain and the N-terminal portion of the thigh domain of CD11b.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the domain swapping experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: CyaA recognizes the segment containing residues 614 to 682 that encompasses the C-terminal end of the last repeat of the β-propeller domain and the N-terminal portion of the thigh domain of CD11b.
source: This demonstrates that CyaA does not bind CR3 through the I-domain and rather recognizes the segment containing residues 614 to 682 that encompasses the C-terminal end of the last repeat of the β-propeller domain and the N-terminal portion of the thigh domain of CD11b.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the domain swapping experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: The 614-682 segments of CD11b and CD11c are only 41% identical at the amino acid level.
source: This finding is consistent with the sequence alignment by the Jotun Hein method (Lasergene software, DNASTAR) showing that the 614-682 segments of CD11b and CD11c are only 41% identical at the amino acid level, compared to the entire CD11b and CD11c subunits that exhibit an overall 61% sequence identity.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis performed by the authors.

claim: The entire CD11b and CD11c subunits exhibit an overall 61% sequence identity.
source: This finding is consistent with the sequence alignment by the Jotun Hein method (Lasergene software, DNASTAR) showing that the 614-682 segments of CD11b and CD11c are only 41% identical at the amino acid level, compared to the entire CD11b and CD11c subunits that exhibit an overall 61% sequence identity.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis performed by the authors.

claim: CyaA likely binds the integrin through a multivalent interaction, making contacts with several integrin segments.
source: Since, however, some other segments of CD11b appeared to be important for full toxin binding to CR3 as well, these results suggest that CyaA likely binds the integrin through a multivalent interaction, making contacts with several integrin segments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that multiple segments affect CyaA binding.

claim: CyaA bound CD11b only when this was associated with CD18 and not when the CD11b subunit was expressed alone on the surface of CHO-CD11b cells.
source: Moreover, CyaA bound CD11b only when this was associated with CD18 and not when the CD11b subunit was expressed alone on the surface of CHO-CD11b cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: CyaA was strongly outcompeted from binding to intact CR3 by the excess of OKM1, VIM12, or M1/70 mAbs that recognize epitopes located between the residues 614 to 682 of CD11b.
source: In contrast, CyaA was strongly outcompeted from binding to intact CR3 by the excess of OKM1, VIM12, or M1/70 mAbs (Figure 2B) that recognize epitopes located between the residues 614 to 682 of CD11b (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CyaA binding to CR3 was strongly inhibited by the MEM-174 mAb that recognizes the CD11b segment comprised between residues 342 to 424.
source: In addition, CyaA binding to CR3 was strongly inhibited by the MEM-174 mAb (Figure 2B) that recognizes the CD11b segment comprised between residues 342 to 424 (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The CD11c614-682b-YFP/CD18 chimera bound different concentrations of CyaA with substantially higher efficacy (on average 24-fold higher) than the intact CD11c-YFP/CD18 complex.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, the CD11c614-682b-YFP/CD18 chimera bound different concentrations of CyaA with substantially higher efficacy (on average 24-fold higher) than the intact CD11c-YFP/CD18 complex and the chimera exhibited only a slightly lower efficacy of toxin binding (on average 1.7-fold lower) than the CD11b-YFP/CD18 integrin itself (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The CD11c614-682b-YFP/CD18 chimera exhibited only a slightly lower efficacy of toxin binding (on average 1.7-fold lower) than the CD11b-YFP/CD18 integrin itself.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, the CD11c614-682b-YFP/CD18 chimera bound different concentrations of CyaA with substantially higher efficacy (on average 24-fold higher) than the intact CD11c-YFP/CD18 complex and the chimera exhibited only a slightly lower efficacy of toxin binding (on average 1.7-fold lower) than the CD11b-YFP/CD18 integrin itself (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The CHO-CD11c614-682b-YFP/CD18 cells were efficiently penetrated by CyaA and accumulated high levels of cAMP.
source: Consistently, the CHO-CD11c614-682b-YFP/CD18 cells were efficiently penetrated by CyaA and accumulated high levels of cAMP (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The segment encompassing residues 614 to 682 of CD11b constitutes an autonomous CyaA-binding structure that enables toxin penetration into cells even when located in the context of the CD11c/CD18 integrin molecule.
source: The segment encompassing residues 614 to 682 of CD11b, hence, constitutes an autonomous CyaA-binding structure that enables toxin penetration into cells even when located in the context of the CD11c/CD18 integrin molecule.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments with the CD11c614-682b-YFP/CD18 chimera shown in Figure 3.

claim: The theoretical isoelectric point of the 1166-1287 segment of CyaA is 3.76.
source: Finally, the theoretical isoelectric points of the interacting segments (3.76 for 1166-1287 segment of CyaA and 8.27 for 614-682 segment of CD11b) were taken into account.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis performed by the authors.

claim: The theoretical isoelectric point of the 614-682 segment of CD11b is 8.27.
source: Finally, the theoretical isoelectric points of the interacting segments (3.76 for 1166-1287 segment of CyaA and 8.27 for 614-682 segment of CD11b) were taken into account.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis performed by the authors.

claim: The CyaAD1193A+D1194A+E1195A and CyaAE1232+D1234A constructs exhibited a strongly reduced capacity to bind and penetrate CR3-expressing CHO cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4C,D, the CyaAD1193A+D1194A+E1195A and CyaAE1232+D1234A constructs exhibited a strongly reduced capacity to bind and penetrate CR3-expessing CHO cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Alanine substitutions of the three positively charged arginine residues at positions 662, 664 and 666 of CD11b almost completely abolished binding of CyaA to the CR3 mutant variant.
source: In contrast, alanine substitutions of the three positively charged arginine residues at positions 662, 664 and 666 of CD11b almost completely abolished binding of CyaA to the CR3 mutant variant and a significant reduction of CyaA binding was also observed with cells expressing the CD11bK659+T661A/CD18 construct (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A significant reduction of CyaA binding was observed with cells expressing the CD11bK659+T661A/CD18 construct.
source: In contrast, alanine substitutions of the three positively charged arginine residues at positions 662, 664 and 666 of CD11b almost completely abolished binding of CyaA to the CR3 mutant variant and a significant reduction of CyaA binding was also observed with cells expressing the CD11bK659+T661A/CD18 construct (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CyaA produced importantly lower intracellular cAMP levels in cells expressing CD11bR662A+R664A+R666A/CD18 compared to CHO cells expressing intact CR3.
source: In comparison to CHO cells expressing intact CR3, CyaA produced importantly lower intracellular cAMP levels in cells expressing CD11bR662A+R664A+R666A/CD18 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: PMA-stimulated monocytes expressed the same amounts of CR3 as untreated monocytes (detected with OKM1 mAb), but bound the toxin with a significantly lower efficiency.
source: As shown in Figure 5A,B, PMA-stimulated monocytes expressed the same amounts of CR3 as untreated monocytes (detected with OKM1 mAb), but bound the toxin with a significantly lower efficiency.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: PMA-activated monocytes bound approximately two-fold more of the activation-reporting mAb MEM-148 than the non-activated monocytes.
source: This was clearly due to conformational rearrangement of CR3 on PMA-activated monocytes, as the activated cells bound approximately two-fold more of the activation-reporting mAb MEM-148 (Drbal et al., 2001) than the non-activated monocytes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Monocytes pretreated with PMA accumulated substantially lower intracellular levels of cAMP upon exposure to CyaA than the non-activated cells.
source: The monocytes pretreated with PMA then accumulated substantially lower intracellular levels of cAMP upon exposure to CyaA than the non-activated cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Activation of CR3 by pretreatment of cells with Mn2+ ions reduced toxin binding and cAMP accumulation in monocytes.
source: Similarly, activation of CR3 by pretreatment of cells with Mn2+ ions (Altieri, 1991; Li et al., 2013) reduced toxin binding and cAMP accumulation in monocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The bent CR3 conformer bound the toxin with a higher affinity (Kd = 2.1x10-7 M) than the extended CR3 conformer (Kd = 6.4x10-7 M).
source: Analysis of the binding curves by a bivalent analyte model then revealed that the association rate was higher and the dissociation rate was lower for the complex of the bent sCR3 conformer with CyaA∆H (Kd = 2.1x10-7 M) than for the complex of the extended sCR3 conformer with CyaA∆H (Kd = 6.4x10-7 M) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by SPR data shown in Figure 5F, 5G and Table 1.

claim: Syk phosphorylation on tyrosine residues was observed after 30 min of incubation of THP-1 cells with iC3b-opsonized zymosan.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, Syk phosphorylation on tyrosine residues was observed after 30 min of incubation of THP-1 cells with iC3b-opsonized zymosan.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No phosphorylation of Syk was detected following exposure of THP-1 cells for up to 60 min to 30 ng/ml CyaA.
source: No phosphorylation of Syk was, however, detected following exposure of THP-1 cells for up to 60 min to 30 ng/ml CyaA, a concentration close to physiological toxin levels (Eby et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Syk activation was not observed when THP-1 cells were incubated with the enzymatically inactive CyaA-AC- toxoid.
source: Similarly, Syk activation was not observed when THP-1 cells were incubated with the enzymatically inactive CyaA-AC- toxoid (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Syk phosphorylation was not triggered by THP-1 cell exposure to concentrations of up to 3 µg/ml of active CyaA toxin or of its CyaA-AC- toxoid for 15 or 30 min, respectively.
source: Neither was Syk phosphorylation triggered by THP-1 cell exposure to concentrations of up to 3 µg/ml of active CyaA toxin (Figure 6C), or of its CyaA-AC- toxoid (Figure 6D) for 15 or 30 min, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: The I-domain-independent mode of CyaA binding did not trigger any CR3 signaling through Syk pathway activation.
source: Hence, in contrast to iC3b, which binds through the I-domain of CR3 and triggers activation of Syk (Shi et al., 2006), the I-domain-independent mode of CyaA binding did not trigger any CR3 signaling through Syk pathway activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Syk phosphorylation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Syk was efficiently activated by iC3b-opsonized zymosan in THP-1 cells that were pre-treated with buffer or with 300 ng/ml of the enzymatically inactive CyaA-AC- toxoid.
source: As shown in Figure 7A, Syk was efficiently activated by iC3b-opsonized zymosan in THP-1 cells that were pre-treated with buffer, or with 300 ng/ml of the enzymatically inactive CyaA-AC- toxoid.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: iC3b-coated particles failed to elicit any Syk phosphorylation in THP-1 cells that were pre-incubated with 300 ng/ml of CyaA.
source: However, iC3b-coated particles failed to elicit any Syk phosphorylation in THP-1 cells that were pre-incubated with 300 ng/ml of CyaA (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CyaA and CyaA-AC- bound THP-1 cells with the same efficacy.
source: Control experiments demonstrated that CyaA and CyaA-AC- bound THP-1 cells with the same efficacy (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and that toxin binding did not alter the level of CR3 expression on the cell surface (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a control experiment supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Toxin binding did not alter the level of CR3 expression on the cell surface.
source: Control experiments demonstrated that CyaA and CyaA-AC- bound THP-1 cells with the same efficacy (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and that toxin binding did not alter the level of CR3 expression on the cell surface (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a control experiment supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: A partial reduction of binding of the iC3b-coated particles to THP-1 cells preincubated with CyaA was observed, as compared to cells preincubated with buffer alone or with the CyaA-AC- toxoid.
source: Nevertheless, a partial reduction of binding of the iC3b-coated particles to THP-1 cells preincubated with CyaA was observed, as compared to cells preincubated with buffer alone or with the CyaA-AC- toxoid (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The cAMP signaling action of CyaA concurrently prevented Syk activation by CR3-bound iC3b as well as it provoked a decrease of the iC3b opsonin binding.
source: Hence, the cAMP signaling action of CyaA concurrently prevented Syk activation by CR3-bound iC3b as well as it provoked a decrease of the iC3b opsonin binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments shown in Figure 7 and its supplements.

claim: When Syk was pre-activated by incubation of THP-1 cells with iC3b-opsonized zymosan, the subsequent addition of CyaA, but not of CyaA-AC-, provoked a significant drop of tyrosine phosphorylation of Syk.
source: Importantly, when Syk was pre-activated by incubation of THP-1 cells with iC3b-opsonized zymosan, the subsequent addition of CyaA, but not of CyaA-AC-, provoked a significant drop of tyrosine phosphorylation of Syk (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Preincubation of THP-1 cells with iC3b-opsonized zymosan did not reduce binding of CyaA or CyaA-AC-.
source: Control experiments showed that preincubation of THP-1 cells with iC3b-opsonized zymosan did not reduce binding of CyaA or CyaA-AC-, respectively (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a control experiment supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The impairment of Syk phosphorylation upon CyaA treatment was not due to decreased cell viability.
source: Moreover, the impairment of Syk phosphorylation upon CyaA treatment was not due to decreased cell viability (Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a control experiment supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claim: Syk inactivation was due to signaling of the cAMP produced in cells by the penetrating CyaA toxin.
source: It can, hence, be concluded that Syk inactivation was due to signaling of the cAMP produced in cells by the penetrating CyaA toxin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments shown in Figure 7 and its supplements.

claim: The cAMP signaling of CyaA decreases the capacity of CR3 to bind the iC3b opsonin.
source: Taken together, our data show that the cAMP signaling of CyaA decreases the capacity of CR3 to bind the iC3b opsonin, prevents activation of Syk by iC3b-engaged CR3 and inactivates also Syk that has already been activated by iC3b/CR3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The cAMP signaling of CyaA prevents activation of Syk by iC3b-engaged CR3.
source: Taken together, our data show that the cAMP signaling of CyaA decreases the capacity of CR3 to bind the iC3b opsonin, prevents activation of Syk by iC3b-engaged CR3 and inactivates also Syk that has already been activated by iC3b/CR3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The cAMP signaling of CyaA inactivates Syk that has already been activated by iC3b/CR3.
source: Taken together, our data show that the cAMP signaling of CyaA decreases the capacity of CR3 to bind the iC3b opsonin, prevents activation of Syk by iC3b-engaged CR3 and inactivates also Syk that has already been activated by iC3b/CR3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: CyaA hijacks the complement receptor 3 of phagocytes by subversively binding to its bent, inactive conformation by binding to a unique site located outside of the I-domain.
source: We show here that CyaA hijacks the complement receptor 3 of phagocytes by subversively binding to its bent, inactive conformation by binding to a unique site located outside of the I-domain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: This novel type of CR3 interaction enables rapid toxin penetration into phagocytic cells and elevation of cytosolic cAMP concentration, thus ablating the pro-phagocytic signaling of CR3 via Syk.
source: This novel type of CR3 interaction then enables rapid toxin penetration into phagocytic cells and elevation of cytosolic cAMP concentration, thus ablating the pro-phagocytic signaling of CR3 via Syk (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: This unprecedented mode of binding and action differentiates CyaA from all other known ligands of the I-domain-containing integrins.
source: This unprecedented mode of binding and action differentiates CyaA from all other known ligands of the I-domain-containing integrins.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: The I-domain is essential for binding of ligands to I-domain-containing integrins.
source: While the I-domain is essential for binding of ligands to I-domain-containing integrins, the CyaA toxin binds CR3 independently of the presence of the I-domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about integrin-ligand interactions.

claim: CyaA binding does not require the presence of Mg2+ ions.
source: This possibility has already been suggested by Guermonprez and co-workers, who observed that in contrast to I-domain-dependent CD11b ligands, CyaA binding does not require the presence of Mg2+ ions (Guermonprez et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guermonprez et al., 2001.

claim: CyaA primarily recognizes the CD11b segment consisting of residues 614 to 682.
source: Indeed, we show that CyaA primarily recognizes the CD11b segment consisting of residues 614 to 682.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figures 1-4.

claim: The CD11b segment 614 to 682 encompasses the C-terminal end of the last β-propeller repeat and the N-terminal portion of the thigh domain.
source: This encompasses the C-terminal end of the last β-propeller repeat and the N-terminal portion of the thigh domain.
evidence: This is a structural description based on the known structure of integrins.

claim: Certain ligands appear to interact to some extent also with the β-propeller domain of alpha subunits of β2 integrins.
source: Besides interacting with the I-domain, certain ligands appear to interact to some extent also with the β-propeller domain of alpha subunits of β2 integrins (Li and Zhang, 2003; Yalamanchili et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li and Zhang, 2003 and Yalamanchili et al., 2000.

claim: The β-propeller domain consists of seven β-sheet repeats that are arranged in a torus, or propeller, with each β-sheet representing one blade of the propeller.
source: The β-propeller domain consist of seven β-sheet repeats (Figure 1A) that are arranged in a torus, or propeller, with each β-sheet representing one blade of the propeller (Oxvig and Springer, 1998; Springer, 1997; Xie et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The β-propeller fold is most closely related to the β subunit of the trimeric G-protein.
source: Its fold is most closely related to the β subunit of the trimeric G-protein (Springer, 1997) and proper folding of the β-propeller requires association of the α subunit with the β2 subunit (Huang and Springer, 1997; Lu et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Springer, 1997, Huang and Springer, 1997, and Lu et al., 1998.

claim: Proper folding of the β-propeller requires association of the α subunit with the β2 subunit.
source: Its fold is most closely related to the β subunit of the trimeric G-protein (Springer, 1997) and proper folding of the β-propeller requires association of the α subunit with the β2 subunit (Huang and Springer, 1997; Lu et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang and Springer, 1997 and Lu et al., 1998.

claim: The β-propeller is followed by the thigh domain, exhibiting a C2-set immunoglobulin fold.
source: The β-propeller is followed by the thigh domain, exhibiting a C2-set immunoglobulin fold (Chothia and Jones, 1997), and by a genu region (Xie et al., 2004; 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chothia and Jones, 1997, Xie et al., 2004, and Xie et al., 2010.

claim: The structural rearrangement at the thigh/genu interface is involved in the activation-dependent extension of the integrin α subunit.
source: The structural rearrangement at the thigh/genu interface is involved in the activation-dependent extension of the integrin α subunit (Xie et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xie et al., 2004.

claim: The β-propeller/thigh region segment of CD11b (residues 599 to 679) can fold also in the absence of the CD18 subunit, since it was recognized by the OKM1 mAb when the CD11b subunit was expressed alone on COS cells.
source: It was previously suggested that the β-propeller/thigh region segment of CD11b (residues 599 to 679), comprising the principal CyaA binding site, can fold also in the absence of the CD18 subunit, since it was recognized by the OKM1 mAb when the CD11b subunit was expressed alone on COS cells (Lu et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 1998.

claim: OKM1 recognized CD11b that was expressed alone on CHO-CD11b cells.
source: Indeed, we observed here that OKM1 recognized CD11b that was expressed alone on CHO-CD11b cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: CyaA failed to bind significantly to cells expressing the isolated CD11b subunit on their surface.
source: However, CyaA failed to bind any significantly to cells expressing the isolated CD11b subunit on their surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The CyaA-binding site within the segment 614-682 of CD11b may acquire the correct structure (fold) only when the CD11b subunit is in complex with CD18.
source: In contrast to the OKM1 epitope, hence, the CyaA-binding site within the segment 614-682 of CD11b may acquire the correct structure (fold) only when the CD11b subunit is in complex with CD18.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that CyaA does not bind isolated CD11b.

claim: An interaction of CyaA with the CD18 subunit may also be involved in CyaA binding to CR3.
source: Alternatively, an interaction of CyaA with the CD18 subunit may also be involved in CyaA binding to CR3, even though CD18 alone was unable to bind CyaA on its own (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a speculative possibility discussed by the authors.

claim: Recognition of additional segments of CD11b appears to contribute to the full capacity of CR3 to bind CyaA.
source: In addition, recognition of additional segments of CD11b appears to contribute to the full capacity of CR3 to bind CyaA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the domain swapping experiments.

claim: Engagement of additional segments of CD11b likely facilitates or stabilizes the higher-affinity interaction of CyaA with the principal binding site (residues 614 to 682).
source: Engagement of these segments likely facilitates or stabilizes the higher-affinity interaction of CyaA with the principal binding site (residues 614 to 682).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the domain swapping experiments.

claim: Toxin interactions at several sites on CD11b would synergize in bringing about the highly selective interaction of CyaA with the CD11b subunit of CR3.
source: Toxin interactions at several sites on CD11b would then synergize in bringing about the highly selective interaction of CyaA with the CD11b subunit of CR3.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the domain swapping experiments.

claim: An initial low-affinity interaction of CyaA with N-linked glycan chains of the C-terminal part of the CD11b subunit is a critical prerequisite for toxin binding to CR3.
source: Indeed, we have previously described that an initial low-affinity interaction of CyaA with N-linked glycan chains of the C-terminal part of the CD11b subunit is a critical prerequisite for toxin binding to CR3 (Hasan et al., 2015; Morova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hasan et al., 2015 and Morova et al., 2008.

claim: A low-affinity interaction with abundant N-linked glycans on the integrin molecule most likely serves as the initial step of toxin pre-concentration from solution into the two-dimensional space of the cell surface.
source: A low-affinity interaction with abundant N-linked glycans on the integrin molecule most likely serves as the initial step of toxin pre-concentration from solution into the two-dimensional space of the cell surface.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous findings.

claim: This increase of local CyaA concentration would increase the probability of proper positioning of the toxin molecule for its subsequent high affinity interaction with specific amino acid residues of the CR3 glycoprotein.
source: This increase of local CyaA concentration would then increase the probability of proper positioning of the toxin molecule for its subsequent high affinity interaction with specific amino acid residues of the CR3 glycoprotein.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the two-step binding model.

claim: This two-step mode of CyaA-CR3 interaction is supported by the SPR binding curves which fit well using the bivalent analyte model, describing a two-step association process.
source: This two-step mode of CyaA-CR3 interaction is supported by the SPR binding curves which fit well using the bivalent analyte model, describing a two-step association process.
evidence: This is supported by the SPR data analysis shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Compared to a mechanism of direct single step binding from solution, a sequential binding mechanism would lower the affinity constraints on interaction of CyaA with the ectodomain of CR3.
source: Compared to a mechanism of direct single step binding from solution, a sequential binding mechanism would, indeed, lower the affinity constraints on interaction of CyaA with the ectodomain of CR3.
evidence: This is an inference about the binding mechanism.

claim: The stability of the CyaA-CR3 complex may be further increased by an irreversible insertion of the hydrophobic domain and of the acyl chains of CyaA into the cellular membrane.
source: The stability of the CyaA-CR3 complex may then be further increased by an irreversible insertion of the hydrophobic domain and of the acyl chains of CyaA into the cellular membrane, which most likely accounts for the observed high apparent affinity of toxin binding to CR3-expressing cells (Guermonprez et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Guermonprez et al., 2001.

claim: It was recently proposed that CyaA can specifically bind yet another β2 integrin on leukocytes, the LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18) complex.
source: It was recently proposed that CyaA can specifically bind yet another β2 integrin on leukocytes, the LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18) complex (Paccani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Paccani et al., 2011.

claim: CyaA does selectively and with high affinity bind the dendritic cells and macrophages expressing CD11b/CD18, whereas B and T cell lines expressing exclusively the LFA-1 complex were recognized with substantially lower efficacy, if at all.
source: However, this is at odds with the initial observation of Guermonprez and co-workers that CyaA does selectively and with high affinity bind the dendritic cells and macrophages expressing CD11b/CD18, whereas B and T cell lines expressing exclusively the LFA-1 complex were recognized with substantially lower efficacy, if at all (Guermonprez et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guermonprez et al., 2001.

claim: The CHO-CD11a-YFP/CD18 cells bound about two orders of magnitude less CyaA toxin than the CD11b-YFP/CD18-expressing cells over a range of CyaA concentrations.
source: As shown in Figure 9A, over a range of CyaA concentrations, the CHO-CD11a-YFP/CD18 cells bound about two orders of magnitude less CyaA toxin than the CD11b-YFP/CD18-expressing cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The difference in binding of CyaA to CD11a-YFP/CD18-expressing cells, CD11c-YFP/CD18-expressing cells, or the mock-transfected cells expressing no β2 integrin at all, was not statistically significant.
source: Moreover, the difference in binding of CyaA to CD11a-YFP/CD18-expressing cells, CD11c-YFP/CD18-expressing cells, or the mock-transfected cells expressing no β2 integrin at all, was not statistically significant (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: CyaA binds cells expressing intact CD11a/CD18 as poorly as cells expressing CD11a-YFP/CD18 with the YFP tag.
source: To exclude the concern that the residual binding of CyaA to CD11a-YFP/CD18 could be due to the presence of the YFP tag, we generated a cell line expressing comparable amounts of intact CD11a/CD18 (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A) and demonstrated that CyaA binds these cells as poorly as cells expressing CD11a-YFP/CD18 with the YFP tag (Figure 9—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a control experiment supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Real-time SPR measurements revealed no CyaA∆H binding to the intact LFA-1.
source: In addition, we purified the intact LFA-1 integrin from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells by immunoaffinity chromatography on MEM-25 mAb-Sepharose beads and immobilized it onto an SPR sensor chip. Real-time SPR measurements revealed no CyaA∆H binding to the intact LFA-1 (Figure 9—figure supplement 3; cf. CyaA∆H binding to CR3 in Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cells expressing CD11a-YFP/CD18 were intoxicated by CyaA to equally low cAMP levels as the control cells expressing CD11c-YFP/CD18, or lacking any β2 integrin.
source: Finally, cells expressing CD11a-YFP/CD18 were intoxicated by CyaA to equally low cAMP levels as the control cells expressing CD11c-YFP/CD18, or lacking any β2 integrin, while cAMP intoxication of cells expressing CD11b-YFP/CD18 was over two orders of magnitude higher than that of the control cells (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: cAMP intoxication of cells expressing CD11b-YFP/CD18 was over two orders of magnitude higher than that of the control cells expressing CD11a-YFP/CD18, CD11c-YFP/CD18, or lacking any β2 integrin.
source: Finally, cells expressing CD11a-YFP/CD18 were intoxicated by CyaA to equally low cAMP levels as the control cells expressing CD11c-YFP/CD18, or lacking any β2 integrin, while cAMP intoxication of cells expressing CD11b-YFP/CD18 was over two orders of magnitude higher than that of the control cells (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: CyaA binds and intoxicates cells expressing LFA-1 with equally low efficacy as cells expressing CR4, or lacking any β2 integrin at all.
source: All these data clearly demonstrate that CyaA binds and intoxicates cells expressing LFA-1 with equally low efficacy as cells expressing CR4, or lacking any β2 integrin at all.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: CyaA was repeatedly reported to subvert FcR- and CR3-mediated opsonophagocytosis.
source: Despite the fact that CyaA was repeatedly reported to subvert FcR- and CR3-mediated opsonophagocytosis (Confer and Eaton, 1982; Kamanova et al., 2008; Lenz et al., 2000), little attention has been paid to the effector molecules and pathways targeted by CyaA-generated cAMP signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Confer and Eaton, 1982, Kamanova et al., 2008, and Lenz et al., 2000.

claim: The Syk tyrosine kinase pathway plays a central role in both FcR- and CR3-mediated phagocytosis.
source: The Syk tyrosine kinase pathway, pinpointed here as the target of CyaA action, plays a central role in both FcR- and CR3-mediated phagocytosis, as it is activated immediately upon binding of immunoglobulin or iC3b opsonins to the respective FcR and CR3 receptors (Crowley et al., 1997; Kiefer et al., 1998; Shi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crowley et al., 1997, Kiefer et al., 1998, and Shi et al., 2006.

claim: Syk is activated immediately upon binding of immunoglobulin or iC3b opsonins to the respective FcR and CR3 receptors.
source: The Syk tyrosine kinase pathway, pinpointed here as the target of CyaA action, plays a central role in both FcR- and CR3-mediated phagocytosis, as it is activated immediately upon binding of immunoglobulin or iC3b opsonins to the respective FcR and CR3 receptors (Crowley et al., 1997; Kiefer et al., 1998; Shi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crowley et al., 1997, Kiefer et al., 1998, and Shi et al., 2006.

claim: CyaA bypasses the Syk-activating interaction with CR3 through a subversive preferential recognition of its bent, resting conformation and by engaging the CR3 structures outside of the I-domain of CD11b.
source: We show that CyaA bypasses the Syk-activating interaction with CR3 through a subversive preferential recognition of its bent, resting conformation and by engaging the CR3 structures outside of the I-domain of CD11b.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Increased cAMP levels activate the inhibitory C-terminal Src kinase (Csk) via the cAMP-dependent protein kinase PKA.
source: The first would be based on the observation that increased cAMP levels activate the inhibitory C-terminal Src kinase (Csk) via the cAMP-dependent protein kinase PKA (Vang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vang et al., 2001.

claim: Csk may directly inactivate the Src kinases by phosphorylation.
source: Csk may then directly inactivate the Src kinases by phosphorylation (Vang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vang et al., 2001.

claim: Inactive Src kinases would be unable to accomplish the double phosphorylation of the ITAM-containing adaptor, which is a prerequisite for recruitment and activation of Syk.
source: Inactive Src kinases would then be unable to accomplish the double phosphorylation of the ITAM-containing adaptor, which is a prerequisite for recruitment and activation of Syk (Jakus et al., 2007; Mócsai et al., 2006; 2006; 2010; Schymeinsky et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CyaA/cAMP-mediated signaling triggers activation of the ubiquitously expressed SH2-containing non-receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP-1 (PTPN6).
source: A second plausible mechanism would be based on our recent observation that CyaA/cAMP-mediated signaling triggers activation of the ubiquitously expressed SH2-containing non-receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP-1 (PTPN6) (Cerny et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cerny et al., 2015.

claim: SHP-1 has been previously implicated in regulation of tyrosine phosphorylation of Syk and in blocking of FcγR–mediated phagocytosis.
source: This phosphatase has been previously implicated in regulation of tyrosine phosphorylation of Syk and in blocking of FcγR–mediated phagocytosis (Huang, 2003; Kant et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang, 2003 and Kant et al., 2002.

claim: CR3-mediated phagocytosis involves active RhoA GTP-ase, which acts downstream of Syk.
source: CR3-mediated phagocytosis involves active RhoA GTP-ase, which acts downstream of Syk (Caron and Hall, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Caron and Hall, 1998.

claim: cAMP signaling of CyaA rapidly decreases RhoA activity and induces dephosphorylation of the actin filament-severing protein cofilin.
source: We have previously shown that cAMP signaling of CyaA rapidly decreases RhoA activity and induces dephosphorylation of the actin filament-severing protein cofilin (Kamanova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kamanova et al., 2008.

claim: CyaA provokes massive actin cytoskeleton rearrangements and unproductive membrane ruffling of macrophage cells.
source: CyaA thereby provokes massive actin cytoskeleton rearrangements and unproductive membrane ruffling of macrophage cells (Kamanova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kamanova et al., 2008.

claim: This inhibitory intervention of the toxin at the two different signaling levels of Syk and RhoA synergizes in bringing about a complete and rapid inhibition of CR3-mediated phagocytosis and complement-mediated opsonophagocytic killing of bacteria.
source: We therefore speculate that this inhibitory intervention of the toxin at the two different signaling levels of Syk and RhoA, respectively, synergizes in bringing about a complete and rapid inhibition of CR3-mediated phagocytosis and complement-mediated opsonophagocytic killing of bacteria.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn by the authors.

claim: CyaA would subvert the central mechanism of innate defense against B. pertussis in naive hosts devoid of pathogen-specific antibodies, thus promoting bacterial colonization and virulence.
source: CyaA would thereby subvert the central mechanism of innate defense against B. pertussis in naive hosts devoid of pathogen-specific antibodies, thus promoting bacterial colonization and virulence.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn by the authors.

claim: Syk activity regulates a number of additional processes involved in the control of bacterial infections by the immune system, including phagocyte chemotaxis, generation of reactive oxygen intermediates, neutrophil extracellular trap formation and degranulation of phagocytes.
source: Besides FcR and CR3-mediated phagocytosis, Syk activity regulates a number of additional processes involved in the control of bacterial infections by the immune system. These include innate immunity mechanisms such as phagocyte chemotaxis, generation of reactive oxygen intermediates, neutrophil extracellular trap formation and degranulation of phagocytes (Forsberg et al., 2001; Gevrey et al., 2005; Mócsai et al., 2002; Van Ziffle and Lowell, 2009; Willeke, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Syk and its homologue, the ζ-chain-associated protein kinase of 70 kDa (ZAP-70), play a crucial role in B- and T-cell receptor signaling during induction of adaptive immune responses.
source: Moreover, Syk and its homologue, the ζ-chain-associated protein kinase of 70 kDa (ZAP-70), also play a crucial role in B- and T-cell receptor signaling during induction of adaptive immune responses (Turner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Turner et al., 2000.

claim: Chemotactic activity and oxidative burst of phagocytes, as well as the Th1/Th2 adaptive immune response balance, were both previously shown to be sensitive to the cAMP-elevating activity of CyaA.
source: Indeed, chemotactic activity and oxidative burst of phagocytes, as well as the Th1/Th2 adaptive immune response balance, were both previously shown to be sensitive to the cAMP-elevating activity of CyaA (Confer and Eaton, 1982; Friedman et al., 1987; Pearson et al., 1987; Rossi Paccani et al., 2009; Weingart et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Disruption of Syk/ZAP70 signaling by CyaA impairs a broad range of processes that play a crucial role in host defense against infection.
source: This suggests that disruption of Syk/ZAP70 signaling by CyaA impairs a broad range of processes that play a crucial role in host defense against infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the known roles of Syk/ZAP70 and the effects of CyaA.

claim: Demonstration of targeting and efficient blocking of Syk activation by CyaA-produced cAMP provides a novel mechanistic insight into the prominent role played by CyaA in mediating immune evasion of Bordetella species pathogenic to mammals.
source: Our demonstration of targeting and efficient blocking of Syk activation by CyaA-produced cAMP thus provides a novel mechanistic insight into the prominent role played by CyaA in mediating immune evasion of Bordetella species pathogenic to mammals.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: This underpins the crucial role played by the CyaA toxin in the early stages of host colonization by B. pertussis.
source: This underpins the crucial role played by the CyaA toxin in the early stages of host colonization by B. pertussis (Goodwin and Weiss, 1990; Khelef et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goodwin and Weiss, 1990 and Khelef et al., 1992.

claim: Vaccine-induced neutralizing antibody response against CyaA is likely to be importantly contributing to protection against infection and colonization by B. pertussis.
source: It further indicates that vaccine-induced neutralizing antibody response against CyaA is likely to be importantly contributing to protection against infection and colonization by B. pertussis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: Absence of the CyaA antigen from current acellular pertussis (aP) vaccines is of concern.
source: Absence of the CyaA antigen from current acellular pertussis (aP) vaccines is thus of concern (Sebo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sebo et al., 2014.

claim: Absence of the CyaA antigen from current acellular pertussis vaccines may represent one of the factors contributing to recent resurgence of pertussis in the most developed countries that use the aP vaccine.
source: It may represent one of the factors contributing to recent resurgence of pertussis in the most developed countries that use the aP vaccine (Cherry, 2012; Misegades et al., 2012; Octavia et al., 2012; Tartof et al., 2013; Witt et al., 2012; 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.
